Image Converter JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF Image Compressor Reduce file size, batch Image Cropper Free-form & preset ratios HD Image Upscaler 2x, 3x, 4x magnification How to Compress Images Like a Pro Image compression reduces file size by removing redundant data while preserving visual quality. Smaller images load faster on websites, send quicker in emails, and take up less storage space. Quality vs File Size Higher quality retains more detail but creates larger files. For web use, quality 70-85% is ideal - images look nearly identical to originals but are 50–80% smaller. For thumbnails, quality 40-60% works well. Target Size Mode Need an image under 100 KB? Enable target size mode and set your goal. The compressor automatically adjusts the quality slider to hit your exact file size target, saving you manual trial and error. Batch Compression Compress multiple images at once to save time. Upload several files, set your quality or target size, and download them all as a ZIP archive. Each image is compressed individually for optimal results. Lossy vs Lossless JPEG compression is lossy -- some data is discarded to reduce size. PNG compression is lossless -- quality stays identical. WebP supports both modes. Choose based on whether you need perfect quality or smaller files. Image Compression Format Comparison Format Compression Best For Typical Savings JPEG Lossy Photos, web images 50–80% PNG Lossless Screenshots, logos, graphics with text 10-40% WebP Lossy + Lossless Web performance, modern sites 25-35% vs JPEG When to Compress Images Website performance: Compress hero images and product photos to improve Core Web Vitals and page load times. Email attachments: Most email servers reject files over 25 MB. Compression keeps your images within limits. Social media uploads: Platforms like Instagram and LinkedIn have file size caps. Pre-compress to ensure smooth uploads. Cloud storage: Reduce backup sizes and save on storage costs by compressing images before archiving. E-commerce product images: Compressed product photos load faster on shop pages, improving conversion rates and reducing bounce rates on mobile. CMS and blog uploads: Most content management systems have upload limits. Pre-compress to avoid hitting file size caps and keep your media library lean. Compression Best Practices Always keep the original file as a backup before compressing. Start at quality 80% and adjust down only if the file is still too large. Use lossless compression (PNG) for screenshots and graphics with sharp text edges. For website hero images, compress to under 200 KB for fast loading on mobile connections. Batch compress before uploading to a content management system to save time. Compress thumbnails aggressively (quality 40-50%) — they are small and fast loading matters most. Re-compress previously optimized images only if you need even smaller files for a specific use case. Common Compression Myths Myth: Compression always ruins quality. Modern compression algorithms preserve visual quality down to 70-80% quality. The difference is often invisible to the human eye while cutting file sizes by more than half. Myth: You should never compress PNG. PNG compression is lossless — file sizes shrink without any quality loss. Many PNG files have inefficient metadata and color profiles that can be stripped safely. Myth: WebP always beats JPEG. WebP offers better compression at equivalent quality, but JPEG still wins for compatibility and is better for photographs with subtle gradients at high quality settings. Myth: Compressing once is enough. Different platforms and use cases need different file sizes. An image for email should be smaller than one for print. Always compress for the specific medium. Compression & SEO Page speed is a confirmed Google ranking factor — compressed images load faster and improve user experience signals. Core Web Vitals track Largest Contentful Paint — hero images that are compressed load before the 2.5-second threshold. Google Lighthouse flags images that can be compressed further — passing this audit improves your SEO score. Smaller images reduce bandwidth costs for your hosting and improve time-to-interactive for mobile visitors on slow networks. Compression Targets by Use Case Website hero images: Target under 200 KB at quality 80%. Use WebP format for best quality-to-size ratio. Product photos: Compress to 100-300 KB each. Higher quality (85%) for zoomable images, lower for thumbnails. Email attachments: Keep images under 500 KB. Most email clients block images over 5-10 MB total. Social media uploads: Social platforms apply their own upload caps and compress images after upload. Pre-compress to 1-5 MB for fast uploads with the least quality loss. Blog thumbnails: Compress aggressively to 30-50 KB at quality 60%. Small size matters more than perfection. Quality Settings Guide 90-100%: Near-lossless. Use for archival, photography portfolios, and print-ready exports. 75-90%: Excellent quality for web. Images look identical to originals but 50-70% smaller. Best for hero images and product photos. 60-75%: Good quality for general web use. Visible only in side-by-side comparisons. Ideal for blog content and galleries. 40-60%: Acceptable for thumbnails and previews. Some artifacts visible in gradients and skies. Below 40%: Heavy compression for extreme size reduction. Suitable for placeholder images, small thumbnails, and low-bandwidth scenarios. Private & Secure Compression All image compression happens locally in your browser using the Canvas API. Your files are never uploaded to any server. Last updated: August 2026 Learn more: Social Media Image Sizes 2026 · Instagram Image Sizes · LinkedIn Image Sizes

Image Converter JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF Image Compressor Reduce file size, batch Image Cropper Free-form & preset ratios HD Image Upscaler 2x, 3x, 4x magnification How to Convert Images Between Formats Different platforms and use cases require different image formats. Whether you need a transparent PNG for a logo, a compressed JPEG for a website, or a modern WebP for better performance, knowing when to use each format makes a big difference. Image Format Comparison Format Transparency Compression Best Use Case Browser Support JPEG No Lossy Photography, web images, social media Universal PNG Yes Lossless Logos, screenshots, graphics with text Universal WebP Yes Both Modern web, performance-critical sites 97% GIF Yes Lossless Simple animations, memes Universal BMP No None Legacy software, raw bitmap data Universal AVIF Yes Lossy + Lossless Next-gen web, highest compression 93% TIFF Yes Both Print, publishing, professional photography Limited ICO Yes Lossless Favicons, Windows icons Universal How to Choose the Right Image Format Selecting the correct image format depends on your specific needs. Here is a simple decision framework: Choose JPEG when: You need the smallest file size for photographs Universal compatibility is critical (email, social media, legacy systems) Transparency is not required Sending images via email or messaging apps Choose PNG when: You need transparency (logos, icons, overlays) Maximum quality is required (screenshots, graphics with text) Lossless compression is non-negotiable Preparing images for further editing Choose WebP when: Website performance is the priority You want JPEG quality at 25-35% smaller file sizes You need both transparency and good compression Your audience uses modern browsers (97%+ support) Choose AVIF when: Maximum compression is critical (50% smaller than JPEG) You need HDR and wide color gamut support Serving next-gen web experiences You provide JPEG or WebP fallbacks for older browsers When to Convert to JPEG JPEG remains the gold standard for photographs and complex images on the web. Use JPEG when you need broad compatibility and small file sizes and do not require transparency. Most social media platforms recommend JPEG for photo uploads. When to Convert to PNG PNG is the go-to format for images that need transparency -- logos, icons, screenshots, and graphics with sharp text. PNG compression is lossless, so the image quality is preserved exactly. The trade-off is larger file sizes compared to JPEG. When to Convert to WebP WebP is Google's modern format that delivers JPEG-quality images at 25-35% smaller file sizes. It supports both lossy and lossless compression plus transparency. Use WebP for website hero images, thumbnails, and anywhere page speed matters. When to Convert to AVIF AVIF offers even better compression than WebP -- typically 50% smaller than JPEG at the same quality. It supports HDR and wide color gamut. Use AVIF for next-generation web performance, but always provide JPEG or WebP fallbacks for older browsers. Batch Conversion Tips Convert multiple images at once by uploading them all and setting the same output format. Each file keeps its own quality slider -- adjust per image for fine-grained control. Download all converted images as a single ZIP to save time. Use the same output quality for batch jobs when all images are similar (e.g., same product photo set). Format Selection Guide Need transparency? Use PNG or WebP. JPEG does not support transparency. Maximum compatibility? JPEG for photos, PNG for graphics. Both work everywhere. Smallest file size? AVIF offers the best compression, followed by WebP. Print quality? TIFF preserves the highest fidelity for professional printing workflows. Animation needed? GIF works universally, but consider video formats for longer clips. Favicon required? ICO format is the standard for browser favicons. Convert your 1:1 square PNG to ICO at multiple resolutions. HDR content? AVIF supports HDR and wide color gamut (Rec. 2020), making it the best choice for modern displays. Format-to-Format Conversions PNG → JPG JPG → PNG PNG → WEBP JPG → WEBP WEBP → PNG WEBP → JPG PNG → GIF JPG → GIF PNG → ICO JPG → ICO PNG → AVIF JPG → AVIF Resize Images for Social Media After converting your image, resize it to the exact dimensions your platform needs with our platform-specific resizers. Instagram Facebook LinkedIn X (Twitter) TikTok YouTube Pinterest WhatsApp Conversion Tips for Different Workflows Web development: Convert all hero images to WebP with JPEG fallback via <picture> elements. This saves 25-35% bandwidth without changing visual quality. Social media: JPEG at 85% quality is the sweet spot for Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter. PNG is unnecessary for photos and creates files 3-5x larger. Email newsletters: Most email clients only support JPEG and PNG reliably. Convert WebP/AVIF images to JPEG before inserting them into email campaigns. Game development: PNG for sprites and UI elements (lossless, transparency), JPEG for textures and backgrounds, WebP for packaging if engine supports it. Archiving: Store original files in a lossless format (PNG or TIFF). Convert to lossy formats (JPEG, WebP) only for distribution to save space. Understanding Quality Settings 100%: Near-lossless output. Suitable for archival or when maximum quality is critical. File sizes are largest. 80-95%: High quality for professional use. Great for photography portfolios and product images where quality matters most. 60-80%: The web sweet spot. Images look nearly identical to originals but file sizes are 50-80% smaller. Best for general web use. 40-60%: Good for thumbnails, previews, and placeholder images. Visible artifacts in smooth gradients but acceptable for small display sizes. Below 40%: Heavy compression for extreme size reduction. Noticeable artifacts. Only use for previews, thumbnails, or bandwidth-critical applications. Privacy-First Image Conversion Every image conversion happens locally in your browser using HTML5 Canvas. Your images are never uploaded to any server. The right crop can transform a mediocre composition into a striking image. Whether you are preparing images for Instagram, LinkedIn, or YouTube, choosing the correct aspect ratio is essential. Precision Crop Controls Our image cropper gives you eight drag handles for pixel-perfect control. Resize the crop area freely or lock the aspect ratio to maintain consistent dimensions across multiple images. Avoid cropping too tightly around faces. Leave some breathing room for social media rounded corners. Use the same aspect ratio for a series of posts to create a cohesive feed aesthetic. For print, always crop at the final output resolution to avoid quality loss from upscaling. Check platform guidelines -- each social network has specific optimal image dimensions. Common Cropping Mistakes Cropping at joints: Avoid cutting off limbs at the ankle, wrist, or knee -- it looks unnatural. Too much headroom: Leaving too much space above the subject makes the image feel empty. Ignoring orientation: A vertical crop for a horizontal layout wastes pixels and looks awkward. Over-cropping: Removing too much context can make the subject unrecognizable or the story unclear. Cropping for Different Platforms Instagram feed: Crop to 1:1 (1080x1080) for square posts or 4:5 (1080x1350) for portrait posts that fill more screen space. Instagram Stories / Reels: Use 9:16 (1080x1920) full-screen vertical format. Keep text within the top and bottom safe zones. YouTube thumbnails: Crop to 16:9 (1280x720) with bold, centered subjects. Thumbnails drive click-through rates. LinkedIn banners: The cover photo is very short (1128x191). Crop tight and keep text in the safe center zone. Facebook link previews: Open Graph images display at 1200x630 (1.91:1). Crop your images to this ratio for clean link shares. Composition Techniques Rule of thirds: Position key elements along the grid lines (or at their intersections) for naturally balanced compositions. Leading lines: Use natural lines in your image (roads, fences, architecture) to draw the viewer's eye toward the subject. Symmetry and patterns: Centered compositions with symmetrical elements create visually striking images that work well in square formats. Negative space: Leaving empty space around your subject creates focus and gives text overlays room to breathe in social media graphics. Fill the frame: Get close to your subject. A tight crop often creates more impact than a wide shot with too much background. Crop Images Privately All image cropping happens locally in your browser. Your images never leave your device. Image Converter JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF Image Compressor Reduce file size, batch Image Cropper Free-form & preset ratios HD Image Upscaler 2x, 3x, 4x magnification How to Upscale Images Without Losing Quality Image upscaling enlarges a photo while minimizing quality loss. Unlike simple browser zoom or stretching, our tool uses high-quality bicubic interpolation followed by smart sharpening to produce crisp, usable results at 2x, 3x, or 4x the original size. Bicubic Interpolation Bicubic interpolation produces smooth, high-quality enlargements by sampling 16 surrounding pixels (a 4x4 grid) for each output pixel. It preserves edge sharpness better than bilinear filtering while avoiding the blocky artifacts of nearest-neighbor scaling. Smart Sharpen (Unsharp Mask) After upscaling, a subtle unsharp mask is applied to enhance edge contrast and recover detail that naturally softens during enlargement. Adjust the toggle to control the effect. 2x, 3x & 4x Scaling Choose from three common magnification factors. 2x is ideal for most use cases, 3x for aggressive enlargement, and 4x for extreme upscaling where maximum detail recovery is needed. 100% Private & Local Every pixel stays on your device. The entire upscaling process runs in your browser using the Canvas API — nothing is uploaded to any server. Upscale Factor Reference Scale Megapixels (1 MP input) Example Input Example Output 2x 4 MP 1080 × 720 2160 × 1440 3x 9 MP 1080 × 720 3240 × 2160 4x 16 MP 1080 × 720 4320 × 2880 When to Upscale Images Print enlargement: Upscale low-resolution photos before printing to avoid pixelation at larger print sizes. Social media covers: Enlarge small images to fit banner dimensions for Twitter, LinkedIn, or Facebook without stretching. Product photos: Increase resolution of product images for e-commerce platforms that require high-resolution uploads. Thumbnails to heroes: Convert small thumbnails into larger hero images for blog posts and landing pages. Legacy photo restoration: Enlarge old digital photos to modern resolution standards before editing or sharing. Website hero images: Upscale stock photos or small graphics to fit full-width hero sections on landing pages without quality loss. Presentation slides: Increase resolution of embedded images before inserting into slide decks to avoid pixelation on projectors or large displays. Digital art portfolios: Prepare artwork at higher resolutions for print-on-demand services that require minimum dimension thresholds. Upscaling Best Practices Start with the highest quality source image available. Garbage in, garbage out. Use 2x upscaling for the best quality-to-size ratio. 4x is best for small source images. Always keep the Smart Sharpen toggle on unless you prefer a softer look. Export to PNG for maximum quality, or WebP for smaller files with good quality. For best results, upscale images that are already sharp and well-exposed. Understanding Upscaling Quality Bicubic interpolation produces smoother results than bilinear or nearest-neighbor by sampling 16 surrounding pixels. It preserves edge definition better than simpler algorithms. Smart Sharpen applies an unsharp mask after upscaling to enhance edge contrast. This recovers some of the perceived detail that naturally softens during enlargement. Upscaling is not magic — it cannot create detail that is not in the original image. The best results come from sharp, well-exposed source images. Severely compressed or blurry originals will not look sharp after upscaling. Source quality matters: A 500x500 image upscaled 4x to 2000x2000 will look significantly better if the original was saved at JPEG quality 95% versus 60%. When Each Scale Factor Works Best 2x upscaling: Best quality-to-size ratio. Use for most general-purpose enlargements — profile pictures, social media posts, and blog images. Results are crisp with minimal softening. 3x upscaling: Good for moderate enlargement needs. Use when you need to convert small thumbnails to medium-sized display images or prepare images for half-page print layouts. 4x upscaling: Maximum enlargement for extreme cases. Best for converting tiny images for large displays, full-page print, or when the source image is very small and no alternative exists. Private & Secure Upscaling All image upscaling happens locally in your browser using GPU-accelerated bicubic interpolation. Your images never leave your device. mainEntity.name: What is the most common social media image size?

acceptedAnswer.text: 1080 x 1080 pixels (1:1 square) is the most universally supported size. Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and X/Twitter all display square images natively without cropping or padding.

mainEntity.name: What aspect ratio is best for social media?

acceptedAnswer.text: 1:1 (square) is the safest choice across all platforms. For feed posts, 4:5 portrait (1080 x 1350) performs best on Instagram and Facebook. For videos, 9:16 vertical (1080 x 1920) works on TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts.

mainEntity.name: Do social media platforms compress images?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Every platform compresses uploaded images to reduce file size and improve loading speed. Starting with properly sized images at 90% JPEG quality minimizes visible compression artifacts.

mainEntity.name: What file format should I use for social media images?

acceptedAnswer.text: JPEG for photographs and complex images. PNG for graphics with text, logos, or transparency needs. WebP offers smaller file sizes but is not universally supported across all platforms.

mainEntity.name: How do I resize images for multiple social media platforms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with the largest required size, then scale down. Use an image resizer that lets you select platform presets — this ensures each output matches the exact dimension requirements without manual calculations.

mainEntity.name: What is the best resolution for social media images?

acceptedAnswer.text: Upload at the platform's maximum supported resolution. Higher resolution images appear sharper after the platform's compression pipeline. For most platforms, 1080px on the longest side is sufficient.

Most platforms accept all three. Stay Within File Size Limits Most platforms cap uploads at 20-30 MB. Compress your images before uploading to avoid errors. Check Safe Zones Profile pictures and cover photos often have circular crops or safe zones. Keep key content centered. Optimize for Mobile First Most social media browsing happens on mobile. Test your images on a phone screen before posting. Be Consistent Use the same profile picture size and style across all platforms for brand recognition. Maintain Image Quality Upload the highest resolution version that meets platform limits. Platforms compress images, so start clean. Why Correct Image Sizes Matter Social media platforms process your images through multiple display layers — feed, search results, shared links, and notifications. Each context uses a different crop or size. When you upload an image at the wrong dimensions, the platform has to guess how to display it, often leading to: Unexpected cropping: Instagram crops profile pictures to circles and feed thumbnails to squares. If your subject is off-center, it gets cropped out. Pixelation: Uploading a small image and letting the platform upscale it results in blurry, unprofessional-looking content. Slow loading: Uploading an overly large image forces the platform to generate multiple thumbnails, slowing down your post visibility. Distorted layouts: Cover photos and banners display differently on mobile vs desktop. Using the wrong aspect ratio creates awkward letterboxing. Common Social Media Image Mistakes Using one size for all platforms. Each platform has unique dimension requirements. A square Instagram post looks different on LinkedIn or X/Twitter. Resize for each platform individually. Ignoring aspect ratio differences. Profile pictures are often cropped to circles (Instagram, TikTok, X/Twitter) while cover photos use wide panoramic ratios. Designing for the wrong shape wastes effort. Uploading low-resolution images. Platforms downscale large images but rarely upscale well. mainEntity.name: What is the best size for a Discord server icon?

acceptedAnswer.text: 512 x 512 pixels (1:1) is the recommended size for Discord server icons. Upload a square PNG or JPEG with your subject centered — Discord displays the icon in a circular crop, so anything near the corners will be hidden. Larger images look sharper after compression.

mainEntity.name: What size should a Discord server banner be?

acceptedAnswer.text: 960 x 540 pixels (16:9) is the correct size for Discord server banners. Banners appear at the top of the channel list and require a Boost level 1 or higher to display. Use a horizontally composed image with the focal point centered for best results.

mainEntity.name: What are the emoji size limits on Discord?

acceptedAnswer.text: Discord emojis must be at most 256 x 256 pixels and 256 KB. Static emojis work best at 128 x 128 for crisp display on all devices. Animated emojis should use the same dimensions but keep file size in check — large GIFs may fail to upload.

mainEntity.name: What is the maximum file size for Discord uploads?

acceptedAnswer.text: All Discord users can upload files up to 10 MB. Nitro Basic subscribers get 25 MB, and Nitro subscribers get 100 MB. For server banners and splash images, keep the file under 100 KB to minimize load times on mobile.

mainEntity.name: What image format does Discord support?

acceptedAnswer.text: Discord supports JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP for most image types. PNG is best for server icons and emojis with transparency. JPEG is fine for banners and splash screens where transparency is not required. For animated server icons (Nitro), use GIF.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a GIF as my Discord profile picture?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but only with a Nitro subscription. Animated avatars must be GIF format at 512 x 512 pixels (1:1) and under 10 MB. For the best quality, use a short looping animation rather than a long clip — Discord lowers the framerate on lengthy GIFs.

We wanted a tool that respected your privacy, stayed out of your way, and delivered professional results in seconds. Our tools work on desktop, tablet, and mobile browsers. ? What People Say SquarePic is used by creators, marketers, and everyday users who appreciate a tool that respects their privacy while delivering professional results. The feedback we hear most often is how refreshing it is to edit images online without worrying about uploads, signups, or watermarks. ? 100% Free to Use SquarePic is a reliable online image editor free of charge. Our team has backgrounds in web performance optimization, computer graphics, and user interface design. We build tools that respect user privacy while delivering professional-grade results — no servers, no uploads, no data collection. * Open Source SquarePic is open source software built by SevenOneLabs . mainEntity.name: How do I make a square image online?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is simple. Upload your portrait or landscape photo to SquarePic. The editor will automatically convert the image to square format by adding smart blur or solid color backgrounds. Then, just download your final image.

mainEntity.name: How can I make a square photo without cropping?

acceptedAnswer.text: Instead of cropping out important parts of your photo, SquarePic acts as an image background extension tool. It fills the remaining space in the 1:1 canvas with a blurred version of your image or a solid color, keeping your entire original photo visible.

mainEntity.name: Is this square image maker free?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. SquarePic is a free online square image maker. There are no hidden fees, no subscriptions, and no registration required. Full tool access is unlocked for everyone immediately.

mainEntity.name: Does this tool add watermarks?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. We are a no watermark image editor. Your downloaded photos will be completely clean.

mainEntity.name: Are my images uploaded to your server?

acceptedAnswer.text: Never. SquarePic is a privacy-first image editor. Images are not stored on servers, and images are not uploaded to the cloud. Processing happens locally in the browser using HTML5 Canvas, ensuring your user photos remain private.

mainEntity.name: Can I create square Instagram photos here?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. SquarePic is the perfect Instagram and Facebook square photo maker. It guarantees your images fit perfectly into the Instagram feed or profile grid without awkward cropping.

mainEntity.name: Do I need an account to use this?

acceptedAnswer.text: No signup or account is required. You can make an image square online instantly without giving us an email address.

mainEntity.name: Which platforms is this tool best for?

acceptedAnswer.text: Square images are ideal when you need to resize images for social media like Instagram grids, LinkedIn posts, Facebook updates, profile pictures, YouTube thumbnails, and product listings on marketplaces.

mainEntity.name: How can I contact support?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you need help or any questions, you can email us at support@squarepic.io. We aim to respond as quickly as possible.

mainEntity.name: What image formats does SquarePic support?

acceptedAnswer.text: SquarePic supports JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, TIFF, AVIF, and ICO formats. You can upload, edit, and export in any of these formats directly in your browser.

mainEntity.name: Can I resize images for specific social media platforms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. SquarePic includes preset dimensions for 13 social media platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter/X, LinkedIn, TikTok, YouTube, Pinterest, Snapchat, WhatsApp, Twitch, Reddit, Telegram, and Discord. Each platform has its specific size requirements built in.

mainEntity.name: Is there a file size limit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the maximum file size for upload is 20 MB. Most photos and screenshots fall well under this limit. If your file is larger, try compressing it first using our free image compressor tool.

mainEntity.name: Does SquarePic work on mobile devices?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. SquarePic works on any modern browser, including Chrome, Safari, Firefox, and Edge on both desktop and mobile devices. The interface adapts to your screen size for a smooth editing experience on phones and tablets.

mainEntity.name: Can I batch process multiple images?

acceptedAnswer.text: Our image compressor supports batch processing -- you can upload multiple files, compress them all at once, and download them individually or as a ZIP archive. The square image editor processes one image at a time for precise control over each result.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Dynamic Blur, Solid Background, and Smart Crop?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dynamic Blur fills empty space with a blurred copy of your image for a professional look. Solid Background lets you choose a custom color to fill the space. Smart Crop automatically detects the best crop area and squares your image by cropping instead of padding.

mainEntity.name: How does SquarePic compare to other image editors?

acceptedAnswer.text: SquarePic is completely free with no signup, no watermarks, and no uploads. All processing happens locally in your browser using HTML5 Canvas, making it one of the fastest and most private options available. Unlike many tools, we never store your images on any server.

About Support FAQ Privacy Terms Secure Local Processing © 2026 SquarePic - Free online square image maker. · support@squarepic.io Support How to Use SquarePic 1. Click “Upload Your Image” or drag and drop a photo into the editor. 2. Choose your editing mode: Dynamic Blur, Solid Background, or Smart Crop. 3. Adjust settings like blur intensity, padding, zoom, and edge radius. 4. Click “Export Perfect Square” and download your image in PNG, JPEG, or WebP format. Common Issues My image won't upload: Ensure your file is under 20 MB and is a supported image format (JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, or TIFF). If you are using Safari, make sure you allow image file access when prompted. The export looks blurry: Increase the quality slider in the export panel to 90% or higher. For text-heavy images or graphics with sharp edges, use PNG format instead of JPEG. WebP offers a good balance between quality and file size. The compressor made my image larger: Some image formats like PNG are already well-compressed. Try using JPEG or WebP format for photos. The target size mode works best when you set a realistic size target based on the original file dimensions. The cropper zoom is not working: Use the scroll wheel or pinch gesture on touch devices to zoom. You can also use the zoom slider in the controls panel. Drag to pan around the image when zoomed in. The tool is not working: SquarePic requires a modern browser with HTML5 Canvas support. Try Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Edge. Ensure JavaScript is enabled and no browser extensions are blocking script execution. Browser Compatibility SquarePic works on any modern browser that supports HTML5 Canvas and JavaScript. This includes the latest versions of Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Safari, and Microsoft Edge on both desktop and mobile operating systems. Internet Explorer and very old browser versions are not supported. If you are experiencing issues, please ensure your browser is updated to the latest version for the best experience and performance. Tools Overview Square Image Editor: Upload any photo and convert it to a perfect square. Choose from Dynamic Blur, Solid Background, or Smart Crop modes. Adjust padding, zoom, and edge radius for fine control over the final result. Image Compressor: Reduce file sizes with either a quality slider or target size mode. The binary search algorithm finds the optimal compression level. Batch compress multiple files and download them individually or as a ZIP archive. Image Converter: Convert images between 8 different formats including JPEG, PNG, WebP, BMP, GIF, ICO, AVIF, and TIFF. Set per-file format and quality settings. Image Cropper: Crop images interactively with 8 drag handles. Lock aspect ratio to common social media formats including 1:1, 4:5, 16:9, and 9:16. Zoom and pan for precise positioning. Contact Us If you need further assistance, please visit our FAQ page for common questions, or check our Privacy Policy and Terms of Service . You can also email us directly at support@squarepic.io .
